extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of history and philosophy of science; readers of Bacon's Novum Organum; historians of early modern natural philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: A close commentary and exposition of Francis Bacon's taxonomy of 'motus' (types of motion) from the Novum Organum, listing eight distinct motions with explanations, examples, and critical notes. Useful for classifying physical/chemical/physiological phenomena according to Bacon's categories and for historical analysis of early-modern natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motus Primus — Motus Antitypiae materiae (Indestructibility of matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion by which matter resists being annihilated; each portion of matter refuses to be reduced to nothing, continuing to occupy place or to subsist by change of form or position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressed by the adage 'in nihilum nil posse reverti.' Linked to axioms denying two bodies in one place and denying penetration of dimensions. Schola sometimes denotes it by axioms like 'Ne fiat penetratio dimensionum.' Examples and discussion note its relation to inertia and historical vagueness in Bacon's use of 'motion.' See commentary on Aristotelian usage and later notes referring to aphorisms ii.40, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motus Secundus — Motus Nexus (Connexion / Resistance to separation; rejection of vacuum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion by which bodies do not permit themselves to be separated from contact with another body; the tendency toward mutual nexus/contact (sometimes tied to rejection of vacuum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by phenomena such as water drawn up by suction or in tubes, cupping (ventosas), and obstruction of flow in perforated vessels unless air is allowed in. Schola called this 'Motus Ne detur vacuum' (no vacuum). Commentary notes Bacon's rejection of vacuum and his equivocation about its existence elsewhere; also points out Bacon's ignorance of atmospheric pressure laws in these examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motus Tertius — Motus Libertatis (Elasticity / tendency to resume original form)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion by which bodies strive to free themselves from pressure or tension and restore themselves to their appropriate dimensions or forms; what modern physics calls elasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: water in swimming, air in flight, oars in rowing, air in wind undulations, resilient materials (strings, leather, cloth), pistons and expelled objects via compressed air. Developed by pressure, traction, bending, torsion. Commentary warns that Bacon misinterprets some experiments (atmospheric pressure) and that this motion is often conflated with Motus Antitypiae and Motus Nexus by careless writers. Also noted as what Democritus and others called 'violent motion' in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motus Quartus — Motus Hylēs (Appetite for a new form / transmutative tendency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion opposed to Motus Libertatis: bodies desire and often promptly assume a new dimension, sphere, expansion, or contraction — a tendency to take on and retain a new form (expansion/condensation leading to transmutations like crystallization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat and cold are the chief instruments: heat promotes dilation and adoption of a 'new sphere,' cold promotes condensation (e.g., ice, crystals, stalactites). Examples include air dilating and then (with heat) seeking further dilation or (with cold) condensing to ice/crystal, and water changing under prolonged cold into a permanent transformation. Commentary links Bacon's account (sometimes erroneous) to later observations on crystals and stalactites and points to experiments (e.g., leaden globe) and relevant notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motus Quintus — Motus Continuationis (Cohesion / resistance to discontinuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not mere continuation with another body (that's Motus Nexus) but the tendency of parts of a single body to maintain continuity; bodies resist discontinuation of their continuity to varying degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manifest in solids (iron, glass) where resistance to breaking is strong, but present to some degree in liquids and gases; examples include mortar after pounding, failure of water to enter very small cracks, limited passage of air through small pores. Stronger cohesion in solids than liquids; experiments measuring strength (tearing bars, etc.) are modern analogues. Commentary notes this is cohesion and refers to experiments measuring cohesive strength and the interplay of elasticity, toughness, and cross-sectional area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motus Sextus — Motus ad Lucrum / Motus Indigentiae (Motion of preference / affinity, adhesion, capillarity, chemical affinity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion by which bodies, placed among heterogeneous or 'inhospitable' surroundings, seek out and attach to more cognate or congenial substances — a 'motion toward gain' or 'need' (indigentiae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes adhesion, capillary attraction, and chemical affinity. Examples: metallic foil preferring certain contacts, mercury moistening metal but not glass, sponges or sugar imbibing water or wine, electrical attractions after friction seen as bodies preferring other tangible bodies. Practical guidance: a canon for opening and dissolving bodies — introduce a proportionate and consenting body to induce opening/relaxation and replacement of prior matter. Commentary cautions Bacon's speculative language and aligns many examples with modern chemical and capillary phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motus Septimus — Motus Congregationis Majoris (Aggregation to great masses; gravity/levity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion by which bodies are carried to masses congenial to them: heavy bodies toward the earth, light bodies toward the heavens — a tendency causing aggregation of connatural masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schola named it 'Mollis Naturalis' (soft/natural) because it appears innate and ever-present; it is perpetual and underlies other intermittent motions. Commentary notes the motion is relatively weak compared to other forces when they operate, explains historical misunderstandings, and remarks that Bacon's observations here prefigure issues addressed by Newton. Also mentions the inclusion of magnetism, gravity, light, electricity, and chemical action under related headings in Bacon's schema.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motus Octavus — Motus Congregationis Minoris (Aggregation of homogeneous parts within a body)
rubrics_metrics.description: The motion through which homogeneous parts inside a composite body separate from heterogeneities and unite among themselves — internal congregation/coition leading to separation, sedimentation, induration, putrefaction, and generation of new forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cream rising in milk, sedimentation of lees and tartar in wine, formation of nodules and flints by aggregation around organic nuclei, two bubbles coalescing, medicinally 'like draws like'. Distinguished from Motus Indigentiae by (1) being less prompted by hostile stimuli and more by 'friendship' of like with like, (2) producing closer unions. Binding of this motion is effected by torpor (inertia), a dominant body's restraining 'fraenum' (spiritus), or external motion; heating can free the torpor. Coition underlies putrefaction (as congregation of homogenea precedes corruption and generation), induration and desiccation (spirit evaporating leads to parts coalescing), and is disrupted by frequent external agitation (hence agitation prevents putrefaction). Commentary cross-references Bacon's experiments (Sylva Sylvarum) and modern chemical/physical explanations (capillarity, specific gravity differences).
